tfn.s: Slow holidays are becoming more popular in Europe.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text does not say whether slow holidays are becoming popular in Europe.

tfn.s: A 2025 Marist Poll found 45% named rest and relaxation as their aim.
tfn.why: The text says: "A 2025 survey by the Marist Poll found that 45% of Americans planning a summer holiday said their main aim was rest and relaxation."

tfn.s: A slower holiday might mean staying in one place.
tfn.why: The text says: "A slower holiday might mean staying in one place rather than changing hotels every night."

tfn.s: The article says everyone should take a slow holiday.
tfn.why: The text says the opposite: "Of course, doing nothing is not everybody's dream."

tfn.s: The writer thinks a short weekend cannot feel restful.
tfn.why: The text says: "Even a short weekend can feel restful if you do not try to fit a week's activities into two days."

focus.note: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a small word. The small word changes the meaning, so learn the two words together.

tfn.why: The text says the survey "does not prove that slow travel is becoming more popular everywhere".

tfn.s: The writer says staying longer is always better for the environment.
tfn.why: The text says: "Nor is a longer stay automatically affordable or sustainable."
Not stated. The text does not say which age groups prefer slower holidays.

tfn.s: The writer thinks a couple with limited annual leave should take a two-week holiday.

focus.note: Many phrasal verbs have more than one meaning. Read the whole sentence and ask which meaning fits.

tfn.s: The poll's result supports the idea that many holidaymakers want to recover, but it cannot show that slow travel is growing.
tfn.why: The text says recovery is "a major motivation" but "The survey did not directly measure slow travel".

tfn.s: The writer believes that seeing many places in a short time is always a sign of superficial travel.
tfn.why: The text says seeing several remarkable places "is not necessarily a sign of superficial travel".

tfn.s: Most of the Americans in the survey took their summer holidays abroad.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text does not say where the respondents planned to travel.

tfn.s: The writer accepts that a traveller who will visit a country only once may sensibly choose a busy schedule.
tfn.why: The text says an ambitious itinerary can be "a rational choice for somebody who may never return to the destination".

tfn.s: The writer treats travelling slowly and staying still as the same thing.
tfn.why: The text says: "There is a subtle difference between travelling slowly and simply staying still."

speak.title: Role-play: planning a week away
speak.setup: Work in pairs. Read your card, then have the conversation. Swap roles and do it again.

a.text: You want to see as much as possible on a week away. You've found six places and a list of tickets to book. Explain why it matters to you, and try to agree on a plan.

b.text: You want a quiet holiday in one place, with nothing booked. Explain what you'd enjoy and why a busy week would spoil it for you.

phrases: I'd love to see as much as possible.
I'm worried we'll be too tired to enjoy it.
What if we spend a few days in one place?
That's a fair point, but we've only got a week.
Could we plan two busy days and leave the rest free?
I'm happy to compromise if we both get something we want.
speak.after: Afterwards, tell the class: what plan did you agree, and who gave way more?
